samples.text:
Nowadays many companies use technology in recruitment. Some people think artificial intelligence should decide which job applicants to hire because it is more objective than humans. However, others believe people should always make this decision. This essay will discuss both views.

On the one hand, AI has some advantages in choosing employees. Human managers sometimes have bias, for example they may prefer a candidate who is from same city or university as them. A computer program does not have feelings, so it can judge all applicants by the same rules. In addition, AI can read thousands of CVs in few minutes, which save a lot of time and money for big companies.

On the other hand, there are many reasons why humans should make the final decision. Firstly, AI learns from old data, and if the old data was unfair, the AI will also be unfair. For instance, if a company hired mostly men in the past, the system may choose men again. Secondly, a computer cannot understand personality or motivation very well. A good employee need skills like communication and teamwork, and it is difficult for a machine to measure these things. Also, applicants may feel it is not fair to be rejected by a machine without explanation.

In my opinion, I think AI can be useful but people should make the final decision. Companies can use AI to check CVs quickly, and then managers can interview the best candidates and choose.

In conclusion, AI is fast and can be more objective in some ways, but it has also problems. Therefore, I believe that decisions about employing people should be made by humans, with help from technology.

samples.text:
As artificial intelligence becomes more sophisticated, some companies have begun using it to screen and select job applicants. Supporters claim that software is more impartial than human recruiters, while critics insist that hiring decisions must remain in human hands. I believe AI can play a useful supporting role, but the final decision should be made by people.

The argument for AI-led recruitment is based largely on the problem of human bias. Interviewers are often influenced, even unconsciously, by factors such as an applicant's appearance, accent or background, which have little to do with their ability to do the job. An algorithm, by contrast, can be programmed to assess every candidate against identical criteria. It can also process huge numbers of applications quickly and consistently, which is a clear advantage for large organisations.

However, the claim that AI is objective is questionable. These systems are trained on past hiring data, so if a company has historically favoured certain groups, the software may simply learn to reproduce that pattern on a larger scale. Moreover, many of the qualities that make someone a good colleague, such as integrity, adaptability and the ability to work in a team, are difficult to measure through data alone. There is also the question of accountability: when a qualified candidate is rejected by an algorithm, it is often unclear who is responsible or how the decision was reached.

In my view, the most sensible approach is to combine both. AI tools could be used to organise applications and highlight relevant experience, but trained managers should conduct interviews and make the final choice, while regularly checking the software for signs of bias.

In conclusion, although artificial intelligence can make recruitment faster and reduce some form of human prejudice, it is not truly neutral, and decisions that affect people's livelihoods should ultimately be taken by people.

samples.text:
The use of artificial intelligence in recruitment has prompted a lively debate. Proponents argue that algorithms can assess candidates more objectively than human interviewers, whereas opponents maintain that decisions of such consequence should always rest with people. Although AI has a legitimate role in the hiring process, I would argue that handing it the final say would be a mistake.

The appeal of automated selection lies in its apparent neutrality. Human judgement is notoriously susceptible to prejudice: recruiters may warm to candidates who resemble themselves, or be swayed by first impressions that bear no relation to competence. A well-designed system, by contrast, applies the same criteria to every application without fatigue or favouritism. For organisations that receive thousands of applications, this consistency, combined with the speed of automated screening, is highly attractive.

Yet the promise of objectivity is, in practice, difficult to fulfil. Algorithms learn from historical data, and if past recruitment favoured particular genders, ethnic groups or educational backgrounds, the software is likely to absorb and even amplify those preferences while giving them a veneer of scientific authority. Furthermore, the qualities that often distinguish an outstanding employee, such as judgement, resilience and the capacity to collaborate, are precisely those that resist quantification. Finally, automated rejection raises a serious problem of accountability, since applicants are rarely able to learn why they were turned down or to challenge the outcome.

For these reasons, I believe AI should inform rather than determine hiring decisions. It can usefully handle routine tasks such as sorting applications or flagging relevant qualifications, but the assessment of a person's suitability requires human insight, and those making the decision must be answerable for it.

In conclusion, while artificial intelligence can reduce certain inconsistencies in recruitment, it is neither as impartial nor as perceptive as its advocates suggest. The responsibility for choosing who to employ should therefore remain firmly with people.
samples.why: Both views critically examined with well-extended support · clear, nuanced position · skilful cohesion and paragraphing · precise, sophisticated vocabulary (veneer, quantification) · wide range of structures with no noticeable errors.
